the best weapon system, from having the best ships, from having the best 
aircraft in the world. After 1956,1 can see that the last three-four years is the 
only time when we have the resources with which we can modernise it, if we 
have the will. But we don't seem to have the will. Part of the reason for that 
is the periodical problems and issues which have just been referred to by 
my colleagues here. I also want to make one point. Why is the defence 
procurement so different? I mean the same set of rules apply to defence 
procurement and to any other procurement in the Government. There are 
also reported scandals in other areas in respect of procurements. There are 
CAG reports, CVC reports and CBI investigations. But the defence sector is 
very different in a very fundamental way. It is this. The markets are extremely 
imperfect markets. If you have the most of defence weaponry, where it will 
go and how it will go, is controlled by the exporting country. You are talking 
about F-16s and F-18s and so on and so forth. 
Secondly, the specification or the kind of defence equipments you need, 
depends on the territory that you have. Both on the demand and the supply 
sides we are dealing with extremely imperfect markets. Then the third 
factor is, there is overcapacity in the defence industry abroad. Let us 
combine these factors. Your demand is specific to your country. I mean, if 
you are a mountainous country, if you have borders, your needs are different. 
The country which is thousands of miles away, the supplying country, 
decides whether you can buy this equipment or you cannot buy this 
equipment and so on and so forth. 
The third factor of this particular market is overcapacity. Therefore, the 
product pricing here is not subject to the kind of product pricing which you 
get in the normal market. This is the economic point which, I think, you 
310 

[27 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
must bear in mind. Therefore, you are making decisions in regard to 
procurement in a market which is highly imperfect, whether supply side, 
demand side or specifications side.  Therefore, launching any set of 
allegations abut procurement is easy because you do require to deviate 
from what you regard as the ideal way. If you are buying automobiles, it is 
easy because you can have whatever you want to have. But if you are 
buying weapons, they are very specific to your needs and somebody has 
to make a judgement, that person — let us assure that there is no corruption 
- even then has to deviate from what you regard is the market from where 
you procure certain other products, simply because on demand side, supply 
side and specifications side, you have a particular need. But markets are 
imperfect. In this particular situation, given the history to which an allusion 
has been made and given the other factors, we must remember that the 
policies of India has undergone a tremendous change. Since 1989, when 
the-Bofors scandal was raised, we have had seven Governments and, 
may be, eight or nine Defence Ministers, with an average tenure of probably 
two years. In the first 49 years, i.e. from 1947 to 1989, we had four or five 
Defence Ministers. From 1989 to 2005, we have had eight to nine Defence 
Ministers. Now unless we depoliticise the whole process, we cannot do 
what Shri Sharma wants the Defence Services to do, which is to procure 
the best equipments in an imperfect market, to do the best for the country 
in an imperfect situtation. You cannot do that. What is the answer? I have 
a suggestion which may not be acceptable to the political leadership. But 
I am sure, Shri Pranab Mukherjee will listen to it and probably will give 
some thought to it. My suggestion is, why not completely depoliticise the 
procurement process. Why must the Defence Minister sign on that file?

ranking. Army people with technical competence, a representative of the 
Defence Ministry at the level of Joint Secretary, the Financial Advisor of 
the Finance Ministry, six or seven or  eight persons at the middle level 
decide on what is needed. Then you have a high level committee consisting 
of three Army Chiefs. They will decide about it. The Army Chief or the Navy 
Chief does not decide on the Navy procurement or the Army procurement 
or the Air procurement. They are wi se men. You have a Bench of the 
Supreme Court which decides all kinds of complicated cases. These are 
people who whole listen to the presenter and take a decision as the highest 
authority in the country. The Defence Secretary may be part of it; the 
Finance Secretary may be part of it and the Cabinet Secretary may be 
part of its. This wise council of six or seven people would decide about it. 
If it needs to go to the Cabinet, let it go to the Cabinet; the Cabinet would 
311 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2005] 
accept their recommendation. Let us set that tradition. But the role of the 
Government, or, the hon. Defence Minister, or, the hon. Prime Minister,

political minds should apply; and there also we can make a mistake, but
